description: A technically advanced Junior Computer Science student with a background in CTF competitions and a specific interest in the security implications of memory management.

nodes.title: OS Structures and Mode Transitions
nodes.personalizationRationale: As a student with strong_prior_exposure, this core content is delivered efficiently to establish the course's theoretical baseline.
nodes.description: Analyze fundamental operating system services and the distinction between user and kernel modes.
Investigate the performance and security trade-offs between monolithic, layered, and microkernel architectures.
nodes.title: Kernel Architecture Trade-offs
nodes.personalizationRationale: Given the student's strong_prior_exposure, we move directly to complex architectural comparisons rather than introductory environment setup.
The student's strong_prior_exposure allows for a rapid transition to process control block structures and lifecycle management.
nodes.title: Process Lifecycle and Control
nodes.description: Explore the process abstraction, process states, and standard operations like creation and termination.

nodes.personalizationRationale: With strong_prior_exposure, the student can analyze the specific performance penalties and cache implications of different IPC models.
nodes.title: High-Performance IPC Analysis
nodes.description: Evaluate the throughput and latency differences between Shared Memory and Message Passing IPC mechanisms.

nodes.title: Threading Models and Libraries
nodes.personalizationRationale: Core required content for all students, leveraging the student's strong_prior_exposure to focus on the mapping between user and kernel threads.
nodes.description: Review threading models (Many-to-One, One-to-One) and the use of threading libraries in C.

nodes.personalizationRationale: This foundational scheduling theory is required for all students to meet exam benchmarks.
nodes.title: CPU Scheduling Algorithms
nodes.description: Examine CPU scheduling criteria and algorithms like Round Robin, Priority, and Multi-level Feedback Queues.

nodes.personalizationRationale: This is a mandatory assessment checkpoint covering Chapters 1-5 for all students.
nodes.title: Midterm Review (Ch. 1-5)
nodes.description: Comprehensive review of Operating System Foundations through CPU Scheduling for the Week 8 Midterm.

nodes.title: Synchronization Primitives
nodes.personalizationRationale: Fundamental synchronization primitives are required for both the final exam and successful project delivery.
nodes.description: Examine the critical section problem, mutex locks, and the role of semaphores in preventing race conditions.

nodes.title: Advanced Concurrency Problems
nodes.personalizationRationale: Explores edge cases in concurrency and lock contention that challenge even students with strong_prior_exposure.
nodes.description: Solve classic synchronization problems like the Dining Philosophers and explore lock-free programming concepts.

nodes.title: Deadlock Characterization and Prevention
nodes.personalizationRationale: Core required logic for deadlock management is mandatory for all students, though scaled to reflect the block's smaller syllabus footprint.
nodes.description: Define the four necessary conditions for deadlock and evaluate prevention and avoidance strategies.

nodes.personalizationRationale: Fundamental memory structures are mandatory for exam preparation and understanding hardware-OS interaction.
nodes.title: Main Memory and Paging
nodes.description: Understand physical address spaces, contiguous allocation, and the transition to paging systems.
Analyze demand paging, page replacement algorithms (LRU, FIFO, Optimal), and the concept of thrashing.
nodes.title: Virtual Memory Management
nodes.personalizationRationale: Core required theory on virtual memory management, heavily tested in final project deliveries.
Investigates advanced memory optimizations suitable for students with strong_prior_exposure to low-level hardware.
nodes.title: Advanced Memory Optimizations
nodes.description: Investigate Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) reach, large page support, and hardware-software co-design for memory efficiency.

nodes.title: I/O Subsystems and Performance
nodes.personalizationRationale: Mandatory capstone content on I/O systems required for a complete understanding of system performance.
nodes.description: Explore I/O hardware interfaces, polling versus interrupts, and Direct Memory Access (DMA).
Analyze file system structures, allocation methods (indexed, linked), and free-space management.
nodes.personalizationRationale: This core block ensures the student understands the persistent storage abstractions used in modern operating systems.
nodes.title: File System Implementation

nodes.description: Cumulative review of all course material from OS Foundations through File Systems in preparation for the final exam.
nodes.personalizationRationale: Final cumulative assessment required to complete the course and verify mastery of all syllabus blocks.
nodes.title: Cumulative Final Review
